title: My rep ranges for Natural Hypertrophy
summary: NH says there is no hypertrophy-specific rep range; total reps accumulated over time is what matters. He details his per-lift ranges (bench and squat 4-8, deadlift and overhead press 2-5, front squat always 5), his own within-range progression scheme ('864'/'543') that adds reps across sets before adding weight, and accessory ranges of 6-10, 8-12 and 10-15, with 15 reserved for four specific movements.

claims.claim: There is no rep range specific to hypertrophy; training at 3-5 reps still builds size.
What matters most is total reps accumulated over weeks, months and years; someone training at 8-12 accumulates far more volume than someone at 3-5, even if the latter moves heavier weight.
NH's rep ranges are fairly high and he almost never goes above 15 reps.
He starts each workout with his low-rep strength work while fresh, since that's where he moves the most weight.
Bench: never below 4 reps because the lift suffers too much from form breakdown; he works at 4-8.
Squat: never singles, doubles or triples, to avoid knee valgus and the back tipping forward; he works at 4-8.
Conventional deadlift: 2-5 reps, never more than 5, because he is confident he can always pull with a neutral back. Overhead press is also 2-5.

Front squat: always 5 reps for usually 3 sets (4 if he fails the fifth), because the front rack position fails before the legs do; high reps let the rack deteriorate while legs are fresh, and low reps waste leg capacity.
Standard schemes like 3x5 and 5x5 felt wrong to NH: either too easy or too hard, and if you barely make 5x5 one week you won't the next.

His bench/squat progression at a fixed weight (e.g. 315 lb): session 1 one set of 4; then 5,4; then 6,5,4; then 7,5,3; then 8,6,4. Once 8-6-4 is achieved he adds 5 lb per side and returns to 4. A failed session is repeated next time.
Deadlift and overhead press follow the same logic from 2 reps: 2; 3,2; 4,3,2; 5,4,3 (his '543').
The scheme lets him modulate volume and intensity without calculations: a single set of 4 leaves room for lots of volume afterwards, while 8-6-4 means going easier on accessories.
The rest of his training, which is the majority, uses only 6-10, 8-12 or 10-15 rep ranges.
Spoto press is 6-12 because you lose a lot of strength on it as the workout goes: 12 on the first set may become 7 by the fourth.
Close-grip bench stays steady for him, so he uses 6-10; most isolation movements are 8-12.
Only four movements go to 15 reps: hip thrusts, wide-grip shrugs, Yates rows and Bradford press, because they use light weight for the movement and need extra reps to achieve the desired contraction.
He never counts reps on bodyweight pull-ups or any calisthenics; he just does as many as he can as often as he can.
